title: Tamar (2 Samuel 13)
hook: a king's daughter is violated and silenced; the text names the wrong plainly

segments.voice: Yesterday, David gets up from the ground after his child died. Your line was I shall go to him. Did you open your hands to something that can't change? A new week begins, and today's story is a hard one. Day seven hundred fifty.

A note before we begin: today's story is about sexual violence. It's told carefully here, without detail, and if you need to stop, that's fine. Tamar is a daughter of King David, the sister of Absalom. Her half-brother Amnon becomes fixated on her. A friend of his, a cousin named Jonadab, hands him a plan: pretend to be sick, and ask the king to send Tamar to cook for you. David sends her. She goes to her brother's house, kneads the dough in front of him, and bakes the cakes. She has no reason to be afraid.
screen: `A KING'S DAUGHTER.` → `A PLAN TO GET HER ALONE.` → `SHE COMES TO COOK.`

segments.voice: Amnon sends everyone out and takes hold of her. And here is the first thing to notice: Tamar speaks. She says no. She says this is not done in Israel, do not do this wanton thing. She asks where she could carry her shame, and what he would become. She even offers a way out: speak to the king, he will not keep me from you. He will not listen. He is stronger than she is, and he forces her. Then, the text says, he hates her, more than he had loved her, and orders her thrown out and the door bolted. Tamar doesn't go quietly. She is wearing the long robe that the king's unmarried daughters wore. She tears it. She puts ashes on her head, lays her hand on it, and goes away crying aloud. That is the second thing to notice: the Bible names this as a wrong. It doesn't blur it or blame her. It gives her words, and it records her grief in public. Then comes the silencing. Absalom finds her and says: hold your peace, my sister, he is your brother, don't take this to heart. And the text says Tamar "remained desolate" in her brother Absalom's house. King David hears all of it and is very angry. The text doesn't say he does anything. Absalom says nothing to Amnon, good or bad, and waits. Much of what follows in David's story grows out of that silence: a murder, a rebellion, a war between father and son. So why is this chapter here at all? Because someone decided her story should be told. In a palace where the powerful wanted it quiet, the text remembers her name, her words, and her torn robe. Her story is told.
screen: `TAMAR SAYS NO.` · `HE FORCES HER, THEN HATES HER.` · `SHE TEARS HER ROBE AND CRIES ALOUD.` · then: `HOLD YOUR PEACE, MY SISTER.` · then, large: `HER STORY IS TOLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to believe someone who tells you. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people in your life who might one day bring you something painful: a friend, a child, a colleague, a sibling. Picture yourself listening, and leave out what Absalom said. Not hush. Not don't take it to heart. Just: I believe you, and I'm here. Say those words quietly to yourself, so they're ready. And if this story touched something in your own life, you can simply breathe, and know that it deserved to be told too. If you pray, you can remember Tamar and everyone like her. The bell holds the time.
Tamar. A king's daughter who said no, was wronged, and was told to be quiet, and whose story the text refused to drop. Today's word.
Your line: her story is told. Today, if anyone tells you something hard, believe them first and ask questions later. Day seven hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Jews read the story of Tamar as part of the book of Samuel; some teachers today use it to talk openly about sexual violence and about believing those who come forward.

let's go to the king together.
fork.reveal: Absalom tells her to hold her peace and not take it to heart. she remains desolate, and the family's silence shapes everything that follows.

original.note: Hebrew: Tamar, the name as written in 2 Samuel 13.

trapdoor: what you thought: a dark story best skipped.
what it means: the text names the wrong plainly, gives Tamar her own words, and records her grief.
what a scholar hears: Tamar's long robe and Joseph's coat in Genesis 37 share the same Hebrew phrase, ketonet passim.
